readings.title: Silas Marner excerpt: the Red House and its two sons (Chapter III, opening)
readings.challenge: Hear how village talk introduces the Cass family before the narrator shows them, and test the talk against the scene that follows.
readings.focus: A great house without a mother, an heir with a secret and a brother who trades on it: the novel’s second plot begins.
readings.context: George Eliot’s Silas Marner (1861) is set in Raveloe, an English farming village around 1800. Silas, a linen-weaver, came there fifteen years before the story opens, after his chapel congregation in a northern town wrongly found him guilty of theft; he lives alone and hoards the gold his weaving earns. This chapter turns from Silas to the family of Squire Cass, the village’s chief landowner. The “war-time” is the long war with France (1793–1815), which kept prices high for landowners. Orts are leftover scraps of food; chines are cuts of pork; a pillion is a pad for riding behind a rider; to distrain is to seize a tenant’s goods for unpaid rent; laudanum is a drug made from opium, sold freely then; “cut off with a shilling” means disinherited. Whitsuntide is the week of Pentecost in early summer, and a twelvemonth is a year.
readings.contentNote: Contains blackmail, drunkenness, threats of violence, and a brother’s sneering suggestion that a wife might die of an overdose of laudanum.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, from “The greatest man in Raveloe was Squire Cass” through Dunstan’s call for ale; opens “The greatest man in Raveloe was Squire Cass, who lived in the large red house, with the…”; closes “…himself across two chairs, and began to rap the window-seat with the handle of his whip.”.

questions.prompt: What does Raveloe say about the Squire and his sons before we meet them? Which judgments come from the narrator, and which from the neighbours?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator explains the missing wife and mother, “the fountain of wholesome love and fear,” and the Squire’s habit of presiding at the inn. The neighbours’ talk (“To be sure, the neighbours said”) condemns Dunsey, worries that Godfrey will lose Miss Nancy Lammeter, and values Nancy for her family’s thrift. Their concern is mostly for the family’s standing and money, which the narrator lets us hear without comment.
evidence: it was thought a weakness in the Squire that he had kept all his sons at home in idleness
Such a daughter-in-law would be a saving to the old Squire

questions.prompt: How does the description of the parlour prepare for the quarrel? What does the spaniel do, and why might the narrator bother to mention it?
facilitatorNotes: Guns, whips and foxes’ brushes, flat ale and a half-choked fire: a household “destitute of any hallowing charm,” matched by Godfrey’s gloomy face. When Dunsey comes in, the dog slips under a chair. The animal’s quiet retreat judges Dunsey before he speaks, and suggests how he treats creatures weaker than himself.
evidence: signs of a domestic life destitute of any hallowing charm
The handsome brown spaniel that lay on the hearth retreated under the chair in the chimney-corner.

questions.prompt: Dunsey calls himself “such a good-natured brother.” How does his blackmail work, and why does Godfrey’s threat to tell the Squire everything change Dunsey’s tone?
facilitatorNotes: Dunsey knows of Godfrey’s secret marriage to Molly Farren and uses it to drain him of money, mocking him with false kindness and even joking about Molly’s death. A confession would leave Dunsey nothing to sell, so when Godfrey threatens one, Dunsey sees he has “overshot his mark” and retreats into “an air of unconcern.” The narrator’s word “hesitating” leaves room to doubt that Godfrey will carry the threat through; readers can weigh his anger against his record.
evidence: Because I'm such a good-natured brother, you know.
there was a point at which even the hesitating Godfrey might be driven into decision

readings.title: Silas Marner excerpt: two opinions at the Rainbow (Chapter VI, opening)
readings.challenge: Follow a comic quarrel in dialect, and notice how each speaker protects his dignity.
readings.focus: How a village settles arguments: by keeping the peace rather than by finding out the truth.
readings.context: George Eliot’s Silas Marner (1861) is set in Raveloe, an English farming village around 1800. Silas, a linen-weaver, came there fifteen years before the story opens, after his chapel congregation in a northern town wrongly found him guilty of theft; he lives alone and hoards the gold his weaving earns. Silas has just found that his gold has been stolen and is hurrying to the village inn, the Rainbow, for help; this chapter steps back to what the regulars were saying before he arrived. Mr Snell is the landlord; the farrier treats horses and cattle; to drench a cow is to dose it with medicine; a Durham is a breed of cattle; a carkiss is a carcass. Mr Macey is the old parish-clerk, who leads the people’s responses in church; Mr Tookey is his deputy; Mr Crackenthorp is the rector. “Pernouncing” is pronouncing, “himsen” is himself, a throstle is a song thrush, and “liver and lights” are cheap offal.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, from the slow start of the evening’s talk at the Rainbow through Mr Macey’s pride in his musical family; opens “The conversation, which was at a high pitch of animation when Silas approached the door…”; closes “…used to be, and there's nobody remembers what we remember, if it isn't the old crows."”.

questions.prompt: Why does the evening begin in silence, and how do the landlord and the butcher get the talk going without risking anything?
facilitatorNotes: The drinkers stare “as if a bet were depending on the first man who winked.” The landlord asks “in a doubtful tone,” putting his opinion into the mouths of “Some folks,” and the butcher answers with a double negative. Neither commits to anything, which is exactly how this company likes to talk.
evidence: Some folks 'ud say that was a fine beast you druv in yesterday, Bob?
And they wouldn't be fur wrong, John.

questions.prompt: The butcher will “contradick none,” and the landlord says “you're both right and both wrong.” Is this wisdom, timidity or good business? Use their words and the narrator’s.
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says the landlord stands aloof from quarrels because all men are “alike in need of liquor”: peace is good for trade. The butcher will not say where he bought the cow but will not quarrel either. Later the narrator mocks the landlord for thinking that paying people to stay away is “dangerous to society.” Readers may still defend peacemaking among neighbours who must live together.
evidence: The truth lies atween you: you're both right and both wrong, as I allays say.
accustomed to stand aloof from human differences as those of beings who were all alike in need of liquor

questions.prompt: Mr Macey’s saying about the two “'pinions” is meant to put Tookey in his place. Take it seriously: what does it suggest about how Raveloe judges people, Silas included?
facilitatorNotes: There is the opinion a man has of himself and the opinion others have of him, and a cracked bell cannot hear its own crack. In Raveloe a man’s character is mostly what others say of him, which is how Silas has been judged for fifteen years. The saying also turns on Macey, whose complacency is one of the things he cannot hear.
evidence: there's the 'pinion a man has of himsen, and there's the 'pinion other folks have on him
There'd be two 'pinions about a cracked bell, if the bell could hear itself.

readings.title: Silas Marner excerpt: a resolution made at night and unmade by morning (Chapter VIII, end)
readings.challenge: Follow Godfrey’s reasoning closely, and notice the moment it turns back on itself.
readings.focus: Weakness as a habit of postponement: Godfrey decides to confess, then talks himself out of it.
readings.context: George Eliot’s Silas Marner (1861) is set in Raveloe, an English farming village around 1800. Silas, a linen-weaver, came there fifteen years before the story opens, after his chapel congregation in a northern town wrongly found him guilty of theft; he lives alone and hoards the gold his weaving earns. Godfrey Cass, the squire’s eldest son, let his brother Dunstan (Dunsey) have a tenant’s rent money, and to repay it allowed Dunstan to sell his horse, Wildfire. Dunstan also knows Godfrey’s secret: he has married Molly Farren, a woman of low standing who drinks, and she has threatened to come and tell the Squire. Godfrey hopes to marry Nancy Lammeter. Readers know what no one in Raveloe suspects: Dunstan killed Wildfire in the hunt, stole Silas’s gold, and vanished. To stake a horse is to wound it on a stake; behoof means benefit; arrears are unpaid rent.
readings.contentNote: Contains the death of a horse and a secret marriage to a woman who drinks.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, from Godfrey’s ride toward Batherley through his doubts on waking the next morning; opens “But by this time Godfrey's interest in the robbery had faded before his growing anxiety…”; closes “…money in his pocket to enable him to keep away still longer), everything might blow over.”.

questions.prompt: Godfrey tells himself, “I don't pretend to be a good fellow... but I'm not a scoundrel.” What distinction is he drawing, and do you accept it?
facilitatorNotes: He will confess that he gave Dunstan the money rather than pretend he spent it on himself, because that lie would make him seem worse than he is. The narrator grants the distinction feels real to him but calls his breach of trust “hardly less culpable.” His line protects his picture of himself as much as it protects the truth; readers may still find some honour in it.
evidence: I'll stop short somewhere
a breach of trust hardly less culpable than that of spending the money directly for his own behoof

questions.prompt: What does the account of the Squire’s “system with his tenants” tell us about the father, and why does the narrator add that Godfrey was “not critical” of part of it?
facilitatorNotes: The Squire lets problems grow through careless indulgence, then turns on people with sudden, unbending severity. Godfrey resents the severity but not the indulgence, because indulgence and delay are his own habits too; the parenthesis shows the son repeating the father he fears.
evidence: he allowed evils to grow under favour of his own heedlessness
for which his own habitual irresolution deprived him of all sympathy

questions.prompt: Why do Godfrey’s arguments for confession, strong at night, fail him in the “still morning darkness”? What is Eliot suggesting about how resolutions are lost?
facilitatorNotes: The arguments seem “tired out,” and only fear is left: disgrace, losing Nancy, and the old hope that chance will save him. He then decides he had seen things “in a wrong light yesterday,” and the narrator reports this as the rationalisation it is. Some readers will sympathise, since confession would cost him everything he wants; others will see a man choosing luck over honesty.
evidence: it was as if they had been tired out and were not to be roused to further work
the old disposition to rely on chances which might be favourable to him

readings.title: Silas Marner excerpt: comfort from the neighbours (Chapter X, opening)
readings.challenge: Separate the narrator’s irony about Raveloe from her sympathy for Silas, and notice where the two meet.
readings.focus: A village’s theories about a crime, and the clumsy kindness that grief receives.
readings.context: George Eliot’s Silas Marner (1861) is set in Raveloe, an English farming village around 1800. Silas, a linen-weaver, came there fifteen years before the story opens, after his chapel congregation in a northern town wrongly found him guilty of theft; he lives alone and hoards the gold his weaving earns. Weeks ago his gold was stolen while he was out. Readers know that Dunstan Cass, the squire’s younger son, took it and has not been seen since; the village suspects a pedlar because of a tinder-box found nearby. A Justice of the Peace was a local magistrate; brawn is pressed meat and pettitoes are pigs’ feet; “Old Harry” is the Devil; “yarbs” are herbs (Silas once eased a woman’s illness with them); the Wise Woman was a village charmer; a Sunday suit is the clothes a man wears to church; “mushed” means crushed or dazed. Text note: this night follows the 1861 first edition, which prints “why, its nonsense” where the transcription has “it's”.
readings.contentNote: Contains grief and loneliness, and well-meant remarks that are also insulting.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, from Justice Malam’s inquiry through Mr Macey’s visit and his report at the Rainbow; opens “Justice Malam was naturally regarded in Tarley and Raveloe as a man of capacious mind,…”; closes “…if he ever knew when Sunday came round, which showed him a worse heathen than many a dog.”.

questions.prompt: The narrator says Justice Malam “could draw much wider conclusions without evidence” than his neighbours. How does the first paragraph explain why no one connects Dunstan’s disappearance with the robbery?
facilitatorNotes: The praise is ironic. Dunstan has vanished before; Godfrey’s imagination keeps inventing “an alibi” for him; and even if anyone had joined the two facts, the idea would have been suppressed as an insult to a family “with a mural monument and venerable tankards.” Respectability protects the guilty, and Christmas feasting dulls everyone’s thinking.
evidence: he could draw much wider conclusions without evidence than could be expected of his neighbours
would not have been suppressed as of unsound tendency

questions.prompt: How has the robbery changed Raveloe’s opinion of Silas? Is the new opinion more accurate than the old one?
facilitatorNotes: Before, they thought him cunning and unneighbourly, perhaps in league with “worse company”; now he seems too simple to keep his own money, and his avoidance of them is put down to “mere craziness.” The new view is kinder and brings gifts, but it is still a theory formed at a distance; neither one knows what his life has been.
evidence: it was now apparent that Silas had not cunning enough to keep his own
was now considered mere craziness

questions.prompt: “Language is a stream that is almost sure to smack of a mingled soil.” Test the narrator’s claim on Mr Macey’s speech. What in it is kind, what is not, and why does the kindness feel “very far off” to Silas?
facilitatorNotes: Macey has come on purpose to tell Silas he stands better in his opinion, and he defends him to the neighbours (“he looked as scared as a rabbit”). But the speech is soaked in his own importance, backhanded comparisons to a calf and a toad, and advice about church and a new suit. Silas, deep in grief, cannot take in kindness of any kind: it falls “as sunshine falls on the wretched.” Readers can argue whether Macey is more comic or more kind.
evidence: language is a stream that is almost sure to smack of a mingled soil
the kindness fell on him as sunshine falls on the wretched

readings.title: Silas Marner excerpt: Miss Nancy arrives (Chapter XI, first part)
readings.challenge: Follow Nancy’s thoughts as the narrator slips into her voice, and decide where the narrator’s own judgment returns.
readings.focus: A heroine introduced with gentle comedy and real respect: Nancy’s rules, Nancy’s pride, and what makes a lady.
readings.context: George Eliot’s Silas Marner (1861) is set in Raveloe, an English farming village around 1800. Silas, a linen-weaver, came there fifteen years before the story opens, after his chapel congregation in a northern town wrongly found him guilty of theft; he lives alone and hoards the gold his weaving earns. Godfrey Cass, the Squire’s eldest son, has secretly married Molly Farren, a woman of low standing who drinks and takes laudanum; his brother Dunstan used the secret to get money from him, then killed Godfrey’s horse Wildfire and vanished. Godfrey still loves Nancy Lammeter, a farmer’s daughter who has turned cold toward him. This chapter is the Squire’s New Year’s Eve dance at the Red House. A pillion is a pad for riding behind a rider; a joseph is a long riding coat; exiguity means scantiness; a horseblock is a step for mounting; a bandbox holds hats and clothes; a toilette is the business of dressing; a tucker is a lace piece at the neckline; a sampler is a piece of embroidery worked for practice; profane literature means books that are not religious.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, from the opening through Nancy’s dressing in the Blue Room; opens “Some women, I grant, would not appear to advantage seated on a pillion, and attired in a…”; closes “…and as constant in her affection towards a baseless opinion as towards an erring lover.”.

questions.prompt: The first paragraph moves from a joke about Nancy’s drab riding costume into her own thoughts. Where does the voice become Nancy’s, and what do her questions about Godfrey reveal?
facilitatorNotes: The grammar stays in the third person, but “you had made it quite clear” and the indignant questions are Nancy’s own phrasing. She says she has refused him, yet she has thought it all out “in their habitual succession,” noticed every change in his attentions, and planned how to avoid being lifted down by him. Readers can decide whether she protests too much or simply means what she says.
evidence: It was very painful, when you had made it quite clear to a young man that you were determined not to marry him
Did he suppose that Miss Nancy Lammeter was to be won by any man, squire or no squire, who led a bad life?

questions.prompt: How do the Miss Gunns judge Nancy, and how does Nancy judge them? Whose judgment does the narrator treat more kindly?
facilitatorNotes: The Gunns judge by fashion and pronunciation and decide that rich country people are brought up in “ignorance and vulgarity.” Nancy judges their low dresses, but argues herself into charity: plain shoulders cannot be shown from vanity. Eliot laughs at both, but the Gunns, who say “'orse” at home, get the sharper irony; Nancy’s reasoning is comic but kind.
evidence: should be brought up in utter ignorance and vulgarity
it was not reasonable to suppose that they showed their necks from a love of display

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator set Nancy’s costly silk and lace beside her hands, which show “the traces of butter-making”? Why is Nancy not ashamed?
facilitatorNotes: The Lammeters are prosperous, but their daughters work: the hands record cheese-making and baking, and Nancy talks about meat pies to her aunt without embarrassment. To the Gunns the hands are a flaw; to Nancy they are simply her life. The detail sets town refinement against country usefulness.
evidence: the Miss Gunns could see nothing to criticise except her hands
But Miss Nancy was not ashamed of that

questions.prompt: After listing what Nancy does not know, Eliot names “the essential attributes of a lady” and then adds her faults. What is Eliot arguing, and why end on those faults?
facilitatorNotes: Being a lady, she argues, is a matter of character (truthfulness, honour, deference, refined habits), not grammar or schooling; the jab at “grammatical fair ones” teases educated readers who might look down on Nancy. Ending with her pride and her constancy “towards a baseless opinion as towards an erring lover” keeps her human and points ahead: her firmness will matter in the story. Readers may debate whether the defence is generous or condescending.
evidence: yet she had the essential attributes of a lady--high veracity, delicate honour in her dealings, deference to others, and refined personal habits
as constant in her affection towards a baseless opinion as towards an erring lover

readings.title: Silas Marner excerpt: two sisters and a compliment (Chapter XI, second part)
readings.challenge: Compare two sisters’ ways of talking, and read a tea-table compliment for what it means to each person who hears it.
readings.focus: Priscilla’s blunt good sense, Nancy’s quiet will, and a parlour where every remark about Nancy is also about a marriage.
readings.context: Recap: at the Squire’s New Year’s Eve dance Nancy Lammeter, a farmer’s daughter who has refused Godfrey Cass because of the life he seems to lead, dressed upstairs while two fashionable visitors, the Miss Gunns, looked down on her country speech. No one in Raveloe knows that Godfrey has secretly married Molly Farren. Blowsy means red and rough-faced; a fortin is a fortune; a hogshead is a large cask; a scrag and a knuckle are cheap cuts of meat; a mawkin is a scarecrow; “sitting on an addled egg” means clinging to something that will never hatch; ear-droppers are earrings. “The old king” is George III, who suffered long bouts of mental illness; to bate a jot is to give up the least part.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, from Priscilla’s arrival through Mr Lammeter’s grave look across the tea-table; opens “The anxiety about sister Priscilla, which had grown rather active by the time the coral…”; closes “…accordance with a favourite saying of his own, that "breed was stronger than pasture."”.

questions.prompt: Priscilla calls herself ugly and says pretty girls “do for fly-catchers.” Is she bitter? What does she think about husbands, fathers and a woman’s choices?
facilitatorNotes: She sounds cheerful rather than bitter: she would rather manage her father’s farm than “fret and stew” about men, and her only husband would be “Mr Have-your-own-way.” She also sees that women with “no fortin” have less choice. Some readers will hear a little hurt under the jokes about looking “as yallow as a daffadil”; others will take her contentment at her word.
evidence: The pretty uns do for fly-catchers--they keep the men off us.
Mr Have-your-own-way is the best husband, and the only one I'd ever promise to obey.

questions.prompt: The sisters argue about their matching dresses. Who wins, and how? What does Priscilla predict about Nancy as a wife?
facilitatorNotes: Nancy wins, as she always has, by gentle insistence: she only wants what is “right,” and offers to wear “a gown dyed with cheese-colouring.” Priscilla sees the will under the softness and predicts Nancy will “master” a husband without raising her voice. When Nancy says she will never marry, Priscilla calls it “sitting on an addled egg.”
evidence: But you do as you like with me--you always did, from when first you begun to walk.
It'll be fine fun to see how you'll master your husband and never raise your voice above the singing o' the kettle all the while.

questions.prompt: Nancy vows never to marry a careless man, yet treasures dried flowers “for Godfrey Cass's sake.” Is she being consistent?
facilitatorNotes: By her own code she is: “love once, love always” means she can refuse Godfrey and still never love another. The narrator smiles at how the grand parlour “exalted her inward drama,” but also says she “was capable of keeping her word to herself under very trying conditions.” Readers can argue whether this is admirable constancy or rigidity.
evidence: "love once, love always," was the motto of a true and pure woman
And Nancy was capable of keeping her word to herself under very trying conditions.

questions.prompt: The rector’s and the Squire’s compliments are felt to have “a diplomatic significance.” What does each man at the table hear in them, and why does Godfrey say nothing?
facilitatorNotes: The Squire is openly promoting the match; Mr Lammeter is pleased by honour to his daughter but stiffly withholds approval until he sees “an alteration” in Godfrey. The narrator explains Godfrey’s silence generously, as the politeness of “reverent love.” Readers know another reason: a secret marriage makes any match impossible.
evidence: reverent love has a politeness of its own which it teaches to men otherwise of small schooling
but he must see an alteration in several ways before his consent would be vouchsafed

readings.title: Silas Marner excerpt: jokes at the tea-table, and a fiddler (Chapter XI, third part)
readings.challenge: Listen to each joke at the tea-table and ask whom it serves.
readings.focus: Raveloe’s comedy of manners: well-worn jokes, a dance claimed in public, and tunes that carry a family’s past.
readings.context: Recap: at the Squire’s New Year’s Eve party Nancy Lammeter, who loves Godfrey Cass but has refused him because of the life he seems to lead, sits beside him at tea; the Squire and the rector have been paying her pointed compliments while her father stays stiffly neutral. No one knows that Godfrey has secretly married Molly Farren. Mrs Kimble is the Squire’s sister and the wife of Doctor Kimble; an apothecary sold medicines and treated the sick; physic is medicine; an epigram is a witty saying; to scarify is to scratch; “for'ard” is forward; to bespeak is to claim in advance. Solomon Macey is the village fiddler; “Sir Roger de Coverley” is a lively country dance.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, from Mrs Kimble’s remark about Nancy’s mother through the call to begin the dance; opens “"Miss Nancy's wonderful like what her mother was, though; isn't she, Kimble?" said the…”; closes “…rising. "It's time to begin the dance, eh? Lead the way, then, and we'll all follow you."”.

questions.prompt: Doctor Kimble credits Priscilla with the Squire’s joke. Why, according to the narrator, and what does this show about how jokes work at this table?
facilitatorNotes: He would rather praise a lady than give his brother-in-law the point: the jokes are small contests between people who have known each other for years. The narrator calls them “safe, well-tested personalities,” teasing that everyone has heard before and no one minds. Ask what such jokes do for a community, and what they leave unsaid.
evidence: choosing to attribute the epigram to the lady rather than allow a brother-in-law that advantage over him
While safe, well-tested personalities were enlivening the tea in this way

questions.prompt: How does the Squire push Godfrey into asking Nancy to dance, and how does Nancy answer? Read her bracketed thought carefully.
facilitatorNotes: The Squire announces in front of everyone that Godfrey has “bespoke her,” so Godfrey must ask or look foolish, and he dreads what his father will say after more drink. Nancy’s parenthesis shows her plan: she will accept out of civility and let him find out he has no hope. Her “cold tone” is meant as a message; Godfrey hardly hears it.
evidence: He's bespoke her for the first dance, I'll be bound.
(If Mr Godfrey founded any hopes on her consenting to dance with him, he would soon be undeceived; but there was no need for her to be uncivil.)

questions.prompt: Kimble jokes that his wife would not mind his marrying again after her death, “not if I cried a good deal first.” How does she take it? Why might Eliot place a joke about a second wife in this chapter?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs Kimble is proud of her clever husband, and at this table it is harmless. But Godfrey has a living wife no one knows about, and in Chapter III Dunstan sneered that Molly might die of laudanum and leave Nancy free to be “a second.” The light joke brushes against Godfrey’s darkest temptation, though readers may decide whether Eliot means it as an echo.
evidence: You wouldn't mind my having a second after you were gone--not if I cried a good deal first?
feeling some pride in a husband who must be regarded as so clever and amusing by the company generally

questions.prompt: Why does “Over the hills and far away” speak to Mr Lammeter? What does Solomon’s choice of tunes show about him and the village?
facilitatorNotes: The tune recalls his father, who used it to say he came from elsewhere, so it carries a family memory: “there's a deal in the name of a tune.” Solomon knows each man’s favourite and plays them as compliments, bowing to the company while respecting “the key-note more.” The fiddler keeps the village’s customs as surely as the Squire does.
evidence: I suppose it's the name: there's a deal in the name of a tune.
he respected the company, though he respected the key-note more

readings.title: Silas Marner excerpt: the dance, and a torn gown (Chapter XI, end)
readings.challenge: Move between the villagers’ commentary from the benches and the private scene in the small parlour.
readings.focus: A whole community watching a courtship, and the two people inside it misreading each other.
readings.context: Recap: at the Squire’s New Year’s Eve party Godfrey Cass, pushed by his father, has asked Nancy Lammeter to open the dance with him; she accepted coldly, meaning to show that she has not changed her mind. Godfrey has secretly married Molly Farren, and his brother Dunstan, who knew it, has disappeared after killing Godfrey’s horse Wildfire; readers know that Dunstan also stole Silas Marner’s gold. Mr Macey is the old parish clerk and Ben Winthrop the wheelwright. Tithe in kind was a tenth of a farm’s produce owed to the church; a sodger is a soldier; “nayther” is neither; “yead” is head; “pritty” is pretty; “piert” is lively; offal here means rubbish; “sniff” and “snaff” stand for a proposal and an answer.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, from the procession into the White Parlour to the end of the chapter; opens “So Solomon, holding his white head on one side, and playing vigorously, marched forward…”; closes “…to get as much of this joy as he could to-night, and think nothing of the morrow.”.

questions.prompt: The narrator says the “Raveloe mind” could not know that a clergyman should be “a pale-faced memento of solemnities.” Is Eliot mocking Raveloe, or readers who expect solemn clergy?
facilitatorNotes: Both. Raveloe treats dancing and overeating as “social duties,” and the dance renews “the charter of Raveloe”; Eliot finds this comic but also humane. Yet she slips in that the rector sells burial ground and takes tithe, which the village grumbles about only as it grumbles at rain. Readers can decide whether the passage is fond, satirical, or both at once.
evidence: instead of a reasonably faulty man
the charter of Raveloe seemed to be renewed by the ceremony

questions.prompt: How do Mr Macey and Ben Winthrop judge the dancers? What does each man’s way of judging show about him?
facilitatorNotes: Macey is the expert critic who finds a fault in every leg and dismisses the women entirely; Ben enjoys what he sees, as he enjoys his ale without “smelling and staring at it.” Ben’s son Aaron asks the most honest question of the evening, about the feather in Mrs Crackenthorp’s head. Ask which of the two is the better observer.
evidence: I don't heed how the women are made
When I've got a pot o' good ale, I like to swaller it, and do my inside good, i'stead o' smelling and staring at it to see if I can't find faut wi' the brewing.

questions.prompt: Mr Macey says Godfrey is “turned round the finger by that offal Dunsey,” and Ben thinks the couple leave the dance for “sweet-hearting.” How close does village talk come to the truth?
facilitatorNotes: Macey has noticed what Godfrey thought hidden: Dunsey has power over him, and the courtship keeps going off. He is wrong about the reason, which is blackmail, not weakness. Ben is simply wrong, and the narrator corrects him at once: the reason was a torn gown. The village sees the surface accurately and guesses the causes.
evidence: else why should he be turned round the finger by that offal Dunsey as nobody's seen o' late
The reason why Godfrey and Nancy had left the dance was not so tender as Ben imagined.

questions.prompt: In the small parlour, what does each of them want? Why is Godfrey “delighted” with Nancy’s flash of temper, and what does the chapter’s last sentence show about him?
facilitatorNotes: Nancy wants to keep her composure; Godfrey wants any sign of feeling, and anger is proof she still cares. His promise to “turn a good fellow” sounds sincere but costs nothing tonight, and the last sentence shows his habit: take the joy now and “think nothing of the morrow,” though a secret wife makes the morrow certain. Readers may pity him or judge him, or both.
evidence: I think those have the least feeling that act wrong to begin with
with a reckless determination to get as much of this joy as he could to-night, and think nothing of the morrow
